All 50 green, ESLint clean. The file is highly refined already — the last cycle required no implementation change (the rounding test passed on activation), so there is no new code to clean up. Let me evaluate systematically.

**Step 1: Naming evaluation (first priority)**

The Green phase added nothing; the names in play are the rounding boundary ones. `roundPremiumInMHPCOsFavour` / `roundPayoutInMHPCOsFavour` — both reveal direction-of-favour intent and the call sites in `quotePremium` and `runClaim` read correctly. `quotePremium` rounds once, at the outermost expression, which is precisely the behaviour the newly-activated test pins. No rename warranted.

**Step 2: Duplication and structure scan**

The one candidate I found is a genuine near-duplication, but the file argues against collapsing it in a comment on `insuranceSum` (lines 248-257): `basePremiumForItems` groups by type, `insuranceSum` does not, and merging them would silently make blocks shrink the insurance sum. That is Rule 2 over Rule 3, correctly decided, and I left it.

**Step 3: The refactoring applied**

One real improvement: `groupByType` was a mutating loop that rebuilt an array on every insert.

content.text:
Refactoring complete. 50 tests passing, `tsc --noEmit` clean, `eslint src` clean.

**Naming evaluation (done first)**

The Green phase added no code — the rounding test passed on activation — so the names under review were the ones the test pins. `roundPremiumInMHPCOsFavour` / `roundPayoutInMHPCOsFavour` state both the direction and *why* it points that way, and `quotePremium` applies the premium one once at the outermost expression, which is exactly the "intermediate amounts stay fractional" behaviour just locked in. No rename warranted.

**Change applied — `groupByType` in `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-08-11_01-07-01_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.6-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts`**

The loop body was `groups.set(item.type, [...(groups.get(item.type) ?? []), item])` — a get, a spread-copy of the whole group, and a re-set on every single item, i.e. quadratic per group to build a list that is discarded and rebuilt each iteration. It now gets the group once and pushes into it, falling back to seeding a new one.

APP mass for the loop body: 15 → 12 (one invocation and one array-literal construction removed; the branch that replaces the `??` costs the same 4 as the conditional it replaces). The mutation is confined to an array `groupByType` allocated itself and never publishes until it returns, so the function stays externally pure — the property the rest of the file relies on.

Worth recording that I took a **worse intermediate step and backed it out**: I first wrote `groups.get(item.type)?.push(item) ?? groups.set(...)`, which is one line and marginally lower mass. Tests and tsc both passed, so nothing would have caught it — but it evaluates an expression purely for its side effect and silently depends on `Array.push` returning a number so the `??` never fires on a successful push. That is a trick a reader has to decode. Rule 2 (reveals intent) outranks APP, so I replaced it with the explicit `if/else`, giving up ~1 mass unit to keep the intent legible.

**Considered and deliberately rejected**

The strongest remaining duplication is `basePremiumForItems` vs `insuranceSum` — both aggregate a per-item figure out of `ITEM_SPECS` and look mergeable. They must not merge: the premium side groups by type first so three alike components price as one block (60), while the insurance side never groups (3 × 250 = 750). Collapsing them into one traversal would read as tidier and silently make block discounts shrink the insurance cover, breaking the cap. The file already documents this at the `insuranceSum` comment; I left both the code and the comment alone. Same reasoning holds for `qualifiesForReducedReimbursement` vs `attractsEnchantmentSurcharge` — identical shape, two independent spec levels (8 vs 5) that are free to move apart.

The two `!` non-null assertions (`anInsuredItemOfDamagedType`, the policy lookup in `runClaim`) are untouched by design. The first is genuinely proven by `rejectUnmatchedDamages` running ahead of it; the second is a real gap — a claim naming a nonexistent policy would crash — but no test drives it yet, and converting it to an error branch now would be implementing ahead of the tests.
